summary: Deep dive on on-prem air-gapped deployment concerns: artifact delivery, offline licensing for GPU drivers, runtime perf (latency/throughput), KV cache & batching behavior, quantization tradeoffs, and VPC/on-prem integration. Discussed checksum/signing for artifact transfer, offline driver licensing, kernel/driver compatibility, and a plan for a 2-hour install and benchmark test.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. we'll wait a minute for Kevin to join, but Luca and I will kick off. quick agenda: artifacts, offline licensing, driver install, then runtime perf — kv cache, batching, quantization.
[00:15] Priya Nair: sounds good, we mainly want to confirm that Redwood can be deployed in our air-gapped environment and what the operational steps are. security is obviously the top concern.
[00:30] Luca Romano: great. high level — our private/on-prem package is designed for air-gapped sites. we provide a signed tarball of the control plane and runtime images, plus an artifact delivery checklist. everything's checksummed SHA256 and signed with our distribution key. you host it on an internal repo or S3-mimic, then we walk you through the install.
[00:50] Carlos Martinez: quick Q — how do you handle driver licensing? our infra uses NVIDIA GPUs but we have restrictions on internet access and we also need offline licenses for the drivers.
[01:05] Maya Chen: right, that's expected. for NVIDIA drivers we provide an offline licensing flow: we give you the driver binaries and an offline license blob that your support team can import. there is a separate EULA/licensing step with NVIDIA — we coordinate but the customer signs the vendor license. we also help with checksum verification and an install guide.
[01:30] Ellen Zhao: on the security side: do you provide signed manifests for every artifact? we need to feed that into our SBOM and attestation process.
[01:45] Luca Romano: yes — each artifact comes with SHA256 and an armored signature file. we also provide a manifest.json listing versions and expected hashes. note — sometimes the transcription in our docs spells it manifest but the file is a simple newline separated list, but it's signed.
[02:05] Tom Hsu: practcially, how big are these artifacts? our transport mechanism is a secure USB shuttle, we have limits.
[02:15] Maya Chen: runtime bundle is typically 6-12GB depending on model variants included. driver packages vary — NVIDIA drivers + CUDA runtime could be 1.5-3GB. offline license blobs are tiny. we can provide a reduced artifact set for initial install — e.g., minimal runtime + a single quantized model to test.
[02:35] Priya Nair: ok. let's talk runtime perf. our main concern is tail latency for small-chat style requests (avg 40 tokens). We currently target p95 < 120ms. is that realistic in an on-prem setup?
[02:50] Luca Romano: p95 < 120ms is achievable but depends heavily on topology: GPU type, networking, batch size, and whether KV cache is warm. For small requests you want minimal batching and warmed KV cache. our runtime supports continuous batching with dynamic thresholds; you can set a latency SLO and the router will prioritize low-latency paths.
[03:15] Carlos Martinez: can you explain more about KV cache behavior in an on-prem scenario? specifically if we run many short chats, how do you avoid cache misses killing latency?
[03:30] Luca Romano: good question. we use per-session KV caching and we support in-memory hot shard caching and optional shared memcached/redis for larger clusters. in air-gapped mode we usually rely on in-node memory with a fallback to a local SSD-backed cache if memory is constrained. cold-starts are the main source of tail latency; we recommend a small warm pool of long-lived worker processes pinned to GPUs to keep KV cache warm for frequent sessions.
[03:55] Priya Nair: is there automatic eviction? what about KV size with long contexts?
[04:05] Luca Romano: yes eviction is LRU with configurable thresholds. we also support compressed KV caches when using quantized weights — that helps with memory but adds a bit of CPU cost. for very long contexts we stream KV segments and keep the last N layers hot; earliest layers are paged out.
[04:30] Priya Nair: you mentioned quantization — what's the recommended profile for a production, latency-sensitive setup?
[04:40] Maya Chen: for latency-sensitive workload we typically recommend int8 or 4-bit quantization with per-channel scales — the runtime has optimized kernels for 8-bit and 4-bit for common transformer blocks. int8 gives a good latency improvement with minimal quality loss in many models. 4-bit is aggressive but can be very cost-effective; we run evals on your sample prompt set to validate quality.
[05:05] Carlos Martinez: does quantization affect KV cache format?
[05:10] Luca Romano: yes — quantized models produce quantized KV entries; the runtime uses quant-aware KV serialization. that reduces memory by 2-4x but you need quantized-aware kernels to read them; our runtime handles that automatically when you pin a quantization profile.
[05:30] Ellen Zhao: any pitfalls with mixed precision GPUs or specific driver versions?
[05:35] Luca Romano: driver/kernel compatibility is important. some vendor kernels for 4-bit optimizations require CUDA 12+ and specific driver versions. we'll provide a compatibility matrix. for air-gapped installs you'll need those driver packages and, importantly, matching cuDNN/CUDA stacks. mismatches can manifest as slow convolutions or kernel timeouts.
[05:55] Tom Hsu: OK — on the offline licensing for NVIDIA, does Redwood sign anything or do we get a signed blob from NVIDIA?
[06:05] Maya Chen: the license blob comes from the vendor (NVIDIA) or from the partnership channel; Redwood will broker but cannot sign vendor licenses. we package the blob and provide installation steps. we also provide a small helper utility that runs local validation (verifies licenses are present and drivers are compatible).
[06:25] Priya Nair: about artifact delivery — do you support partial installs for testing? we don't want to deploy the entire cluster first.
[06:35] Luca Romano: absolutely. we provide a "smoke" bundle: core runtime, a single model (quantized), and a local benchmark harness. that's what we recommend for the 2-hour install window. After that we can deliver additional model variants/binaries.
[06:55] Carlos Martinez: the install script — is it an interactive installer requiring outbound internet? we can't allow that.
[07:05] Maya Chen: no outbound calls. the installer has an interactive offline mode. it looks for artifact dirs, verifies signatures, unpacks, registers services with systemd or k8s manifests (we support both bare metal + k8s), and runs a local health-check. we log every step with a signed run manifest so your security team can archive it.
[07:30] Priya Nair: nice. let's go deeper on batching thresholds. Our traffic is bursty — multi-tenant chat across departments. How do you configure batching to avoid latency spikes?
[07:45] Luca Romano: we have adaptive batching: the runtime accumulates requests up to a max batch size or a latency deadline. for low-latency you lower the deadline (e.g. 10ms) and use smaller max batch sizes. we also support preemptive draining for high-priority requests. another lever is dynamic routing: route small, latency-sensitive requests to a dedicated pool with smaller batch windows, and background jobs to a high-throughput pool.
[08:15] Carlos Martinez: how does that interact with cost? smaller batches mean lower GPU utilization.
[08:20] Maya Chen: correct — that's the tradeoff. we provide Optimize recommendations: for example, keep a small dedicated pool pinned for p95 latency and a larger autoscaling pool for throughput. caching helps a lot — if KV cache hits are high, token compute is lower and small batches are cheaper. quantization further reduces token cost.
[08:45] Tom Hsu: can you give ballpark numbers? like tokens/sec on an A40 versus H100 for a 7B model with int8, 40-token response?
[08:55] Luca Romano: rough numbers — a 7B int8 on H100: ~700-1200 tokens/sec depending on sequence length; on an A40 maybe ~220-400 tokens/sec. for 40-token p95 with warm KV and small batch sizes we can hit sub-120ms on H100; A40 will be higher. But these are ballparks — we'll run your benchmark.
[09:25] Priya Nair: thanks. for our environment we have mostly A40s and some older V100s; would you recommend Dedicated hardware through Redwood or bring-your-own on-prem?
[09:40] Maya Chen: for enterprise with strict data residency, bring-your-own on-prem is common. Redwood Private runs on your fleet, we just ship artifacts. If you want predictable throughput and we'd manage the fleet, Redwood Dedicated (colocated) is an option but that's more of a hosted/dedicated offering. Since you're air-gapped, Private is the expected path.
[09:55] Carlos Martinez: operational question: how do rolling updates work offline? we need to keep services up, apply updates without internet.
[10:05] Luca Romano: we provide staged bundles and a canary/update controller that works fully offline. the update controller applies the new bundle to a subset of nodes, runs health checks, and then promotes. The controller relies on local artifact repo and signed manifests to validate updates.
[10:25] Ellen Zhao: audit logs — will we get local logs and a way to export them for SOC2?
[10:32] Maya Chen: yes; we emit structured logs and audit events (RBAC changes, model loads, license installs). all logs are local and we provide a log forwarding config if you have internal SIEM. also per-route token breakdowns for cost accounting.
[10:50] Tom Hsu: a couple of gotchas we've seen: GPU driver mismatches cause silent slowdowns and sometimes CUDA kernel timeouts. do you have a recommended test to catch that quickly?
[11:00] Luca Romano: our installation smoke test includes microbenchmarks that exercise critical kernels and a short LLM prompt set. it verifies throughput and runs a kernel sanity check; if it detects a mismatch it reports driver/runtime version mismatches and recommended steps.
[11:20] Priya Nair: good. about model rollouts — can we A/B test new quant profiles?
[11:30] Maya Chen: yes, our rollout supports canarying by model version and quant profile. you can route a percent traffic and monitor quality metrics (we integrate with your eval harness or use Redwood's eval set). if quality regresses we can auto-roll back.
[11:50] Carlos Martinez: one more on KV: do you persist KV caches across restarts? on worker restart we lose warm cache; that impacts latency.
[11:58] Luca Romano: we persist a checkpointed snapshot of hot KV to local SSD periodically; on restart the runtime will warm from the snapshot. but there's always a warm-up period for new sessions. for very strict p95 you keep pinned processes.
[12:20] Kevin Li: (joined) apologies for the delay. quick ask — what's the support model during install?
[12:28] Maya Chen: we offer a runbook-based install support. for air-gapped installs we provide a two-hour remote co-install session with an SE on-call; if you want onsite, that's part of the enterprise engagement. we'll also provide a dedicated slack or ticket channel for the installer.
[12:45] Kevin Li: timeline-wise, we need a pilot in April. possible?
[12:50] Maya Chen: yes — if we deliver smoke artifacts this week and you confirm a 2-hour window for the install before end of March, we can run the pilot in early April.
[13:05] Priya Nair: how do we validate quality after quantizing? you mentioned evals — what's the flow?
[13:12] Luca Romano: we run a diff eval on your sample prompts comparing baseline FP16 vs quant profiles. we provide metrics: BLEU-ish, token-level perplexity, LLM-specific metrics, and human-assigned judge scores if needed. we produce a regression report and recommend which quant profile passes your quality bar.
[13:35] Carlos Martinez: are there any legal steps for offline licensing that we should prep?
[13:40] Maya Chen: typically you sign the GPU vendor agreement; Redwood assists with contact and the process for offline license procurement. we also provide an MSA addendum for Private deployments covering artifact handling and support.
[13:55] Ellen Zhao: for attestation, we need signed manifests for the exact binaries installed and a way to verify signatures offline. you covered that but can you include the GPG public key fingerprint in the deliverable?
[14:05] Luca Romano: yes we'll include the distribution public key fingerprint and instructions to pin it in your attestation tooling.
[14:20] Tom Hsu: final thing — can we run a short perf run now or do we need the artifact?
[14:28] Luca Romano: we can only run microbenchmarks locally if you have the smoke bundle. we cannot run meaningful perf without the runtime binaries and model.
[14:35] Priya Nair: ok let's recap next steps.
[14:40] Maya Chen: recap: Luca will send the artifact delivery checklist + SHA instructions; Maya will send offline licensing steps and vendor contact; Sentinel will confirm 2-hour install window and provide sample prompts and GPU inventory; we'll schedule the smoke install and a benchmark run.
[14:55] Kevin Li: that works. please also include pricing options.
[15:00] Maya Chen: will do. thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the checklist in a separate email and attach the baseline benchmark template."
